title: The Letter of Jeremiah: They Are Not Gods
sum: The last chapter of Baruch in Catholic Bibles, and a separate book in Greek and Orthodox Bibles, is a letter in Jeremiah's name to the people about to be taken to Babylon. It warns them that they will stay "as long as seven generations" (6:2) and will see gods of silver, gold and wood carried through the streets while crowds bow down. They must not copy the foreigners or fear those gods. Instead they are to say in their minds, "You are the one we must worship, Master" (6:5).

The rest is a long, mocking list of what the gods cannot do. They gather dust and soot, bats and cats sit on them, their priests steal from them, they cannot stand up when they fall, cannot rescue anyone, cannot send rain or set up a king, and burn like beams when the temple catches fire. In some ten places a refrain sums up: they are not gods, so do not fear them. The letter ends with the only use of the word 'idols': the righteous person who keeps none is better off (6:72).
readings: Read as a letter of the prophet

Read as its heading presents it, the letter is Jeremiah's word to the first captives. Tertullian quoted 6:5 as Jeremiah's (Scorpiace 8), and Athanasius counted "the epistle" with Jeremiah among the books of the Old Testament (Festal Letter 39). Francis Gigot, in the Catholic Encyclopedia, says the letter's own title has long been the reason for the "time-honoured view" that the prophet wrote it; he reports the critics' doubts without settling the question, and says the Church has always received the chapter as inspired. Read this way, the two letters of Jeremiah do different work: Jeremiah 29 tells the exiles to settle in Babylon, and this one tells them not to give their worship to its gods.
Read as a later Jewish tract

Read as a work written later in Jeremiah's name, as Sean Adams and the other scholars cited on this page read it, the letter is a sermon for Jews living among the temples and festivals of a foreign land. Adams puts a Hebrew original, if there was one, between the 500s and the first century BC, and the Greek after Alexander, probably in the 200s or 100s BC (see "Who wrote it, and when" below). Its argument is built from Jeremiah 10 and Isaiah 44, and its purpose is the same in any century: to keep a minority from being drawn in by the religion of the majority around them.

views.C: Catholic Bibles follow the Latin Vulgate, which makes the letter the sixth chapter of Baruch, and read it as inspired Scripture. Its use in the early Latin church is old: Tertullian quoted 6:5 as Jeremiah's words to Christians facing death for refusing to worship the gods (Scorpiace 8).
views.O: Orthodox Bibles keep the Greek arrangement, with the Letter as its own book after Lamentations. Athanasius' list of 367 counts "Jeremiah with Baruch, Lamentations, and the epistle, one book" among the books of the Old Testament (Festal Letter 39).
views.P: Protestant churches set the letter among the Apocrypha. The Church of England's Article VI lists "Baruch the Prophet" (whose sixth chapter in the KJV is this letter) among the books the church reads "for example of life and instruction of manners" but does not use "to establish any doctrine". The Westminster Confession (1.3) is stricter: the books called Apocrypha are not of divine inspiration, are no part of the canon, and may be used only as other human writings. The Bible's own letter of Jeremiah to the exiles is Jeremiah 29.
views.H: Historians date the letter by three markers: its "seven generations" (6:2), which Daniel Harrington counts to about 317 BC; the allusion in 2 Maccabees 2:2; and the Qumran papyrus 7Q2, which Harrington dates about 100 BC. From the last two he takes the 100s BC as the latest possible date. Sean Adams puts a Hebrew original, if there was one, between the 500s and the first century BC and the Greek after Alexander, likely in the 200s or 100s BC; he notes that 7Q2 has only twenty-two letters, so its identification is not certain. Whether the letter was written in Hebrew or Greek is debated: Carey Moore argued for a Hebrew original from apparent misreadings (6:11, 6:54, 6:71), while Benjamin Wright finds the evidence inconclusive, since the Greek has many features of a text composed in Greek.
views.J: The letter is not in the Jewish Bible. But the idea behind it is known in Jewish reading of Jeremiah: Rashi (in the Judaica Press translation by A. J. Rosenberg) says the Aramaic verse Jeremiah 10:11 is a letter Jeremiah sent to King Jeconiah and the exiles, so that they could answer the Chaldeans if they were told to worship idols. Claude's observation, not Rashi's: the Letter of Jeremiah reads like a long form of that same picture, though Rashi does not mention it.

deep.b:
The letter has no story and almost no description of God. It works by piling up observations, each ending in a refrain. The gods are made (6:7, 6:45), so they are less than their makers. They must be carried, dressed, cleaned, locked up and fed (6:12–27), so they are served rather than serving. They cannot do what a god does: punish, reward, crown a king, send rain, rescue the poor, show signs in the sky (6:33–37, 6:52–53, 6:66). Things that are only creatures, the sun, moon, stars, lightning, wind, clouds and fire, at least obey God (6:59–62); the gods do not even do that. Even a door, a pot or a post is more useful (6:58).

Every one of these points has a root in the 66 books: Jeremiah 10:1–16, Isaiah 40:18–20 and 44:9–20, Isaiah 46:1–7, Psalm 115:4–8 and Psalm 135:15–18, Habakkuk 2:18–19. The letter adds detail from life among the temples: bats and cats, soot on the faces, priests in mourning, women with cords in the street. Like the prophets, it is satire. As this site's notes on Isaiah 44 and Jeremiah 10 explain, Babylon's priests held that a god chose to be present in its consecrated image, and the letter does not try to answer that belief. Its aim is to keep Jews from fearing the gods, not to describe them fairly.

The heading names Jeremiah, and the letter is set at the start of the exile (6:1–2). Scholars weigh four pieces of evidence. The writer knows Jeremiah 10 in Hebrew, since the scarecrow of 6:69 is in the Hebrew of Jeremiah 10:5 but not in its Greek (Wright). His "seven generations" (6:2) stretch Jeremiah's seventy years: counting forty years to a generation, Daniel Harrington reaches about 317 BC, and David deSilva reports scholars who take 317–306 BC as the latest date for a Hebrew original, while warning that a generation is too loose a measure for precision (see 6:2). 2 Maccabees 2:2 says Jeremiah told the deported "not to let their minds be led astray when they saw images of gold and silver and the finery on them" (2 Maccabees 2:2), which sounds like this letter, though it does not quote it; Sean Adams notes that it may not refer to the Letter at all, and that Dimant has suggested it draws on a Qumran work, the Apocryphon of Jeremiah C, instead. And the papyrus 7Q2, if it is the Letter, shows a Greek copy by about 100 BC (Harrington's date; Adams on its uncertainty, see 6:44).

From these Harrington takes the 100s BC as the latest possible date, and Adams puts a Hebrew original, if there was one, between the 500s and the first century BC and the Greek after Alexander, likely in the 200s or 100s BC. Where it was written is unknown: Adams lists Egypt (Alexandria), Babylon and Palestine as proposals. Harrington thinks a Hebrew original would fit the land of Israel at a time hostile to foreign cults, perhaps under Antiochus IV, but notes that the writer knows Babylonian customs well and may have written in Babylon earlier. If Budin is right that the women with cords of 6:42–43 come from Herodotus, the letter is later than Herodotus.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a refrain for people who could not leave
deep.b: My own suggestion. Jeremiah's real letter told the exiles to stay: "Build houses and settle in them" (Jeremiah 29:5). A community that stays for "seven generations" faces a harder problem than a few years' captivity: the festivals come round every spring, the children grow up with them, and fear becomes habit. The letter's answer is not to leave, or to fight, but a single sentence said silently in the crowd (6:5), and a refrain that can be memorized. Read this way, the letter is less an argument for outsiders than a drill for insiders: a way of seeing the procession that makes it lose its power. This is my reading of the letter's form; it fits the settings scholars propose, but I have not seen it argued in this form.

echoes: Jeremiah 10:1–16; Jeremiah 29:1–23; Isaiah 44:9–20; Isaiah 46:1–7; Psalm 115:4–8; Psalm 135:15–18; Habakkuk 2:18–19; Deuteronomy 4:28; Daniel 3; 2 Maccabees 2:1–3; Wisdom of Solomon 13:10–19; Additions to Daniel; Acts 19:26; 1 Corinthians 8:4; 1 Corinthians 10:19–20; Revelation 9:20; 1 John 5:21

settings.what: The Letter of Jeremiah, against the gods of Babylon
settings.by: Jeremiah, as the heading presents him, writing what God ordered him to say
settings.to: The people of Judah "about to be led off as captives to Babylon" (6:1), before the deportation
settings.when: On the eve of the exile under Nebuchadnezzar, as the letter sets it (597 or 586 BC)
settings.why: Inside the letter's own setting: to prepare captives for the sight of Babylon's gods carried through the streets and worshiped by crowds, so that they do not copy the foreigners or fear the gods, and keep worshiping the Master silently in the crowd (6:4–5). Each section strips the gods of one power, so that by the end fear has nothing left to hold on to. For the letter's real first readers, whose date and place are debated (see the views), the same words were a guide for living as a minority among foreign temples.
settings.readers: Jews living as a minority among foreign temples in the centuries before Jesus, addressed by a writer who judges by Israel's purity laws (6:28) and knew Jeremiah 10 in Hebrew (6:69, as Wright notes). If the Qumran papyrus 7Q2 is this letter, it was copied in Greek by about 100 BC (Harrington's date) and kept at Qumran; the fragment is small and the identification is not certain (Adams).
views: Daniel Harrington notes that the writer knows Babylonian customs well and may have written in Babylon; Sean Adams lists Babylon among the proposed places.

Harrington: if the letter was composed in Hebrew, a setting in the land of Israel at a time hostile to foreign cults, perhaps the crisis under Antiochus IV Epiphanes, seems likely. Adams lists Palestine among the proposals.

Adams lists Egypt, specifically Alexandria, among the proposed places of writing; on that view the readers were Greek-speaking Jews among Egypt's temples. Budin's argument that 6:42–43 draws on Herodotus concerns the source of one detail, not where the readers lived.
Read as the heading presents it, and as Tertullian quoted it, as Jeremiah's words, the first readers are the exiles of 597 or 586 BC themselves.

settings.by: The captives, as the letter tells them to pray
settings.when: While the crowds bow before the gods in procession
settings.why: A one-line confession said in the mind, not aloud, so that a captive can stand in the crowd without giving worship to its gods. It turns the outward scene inside out: the crowd bows, but the one who must be worshiped is the Master.
settings.readers: The letter's Jewish readers; later, Christians under persecution, to whom Tertullian quoted it about AD 211 (Scorpiace 8).
